title: Options
intro: An option gives its owner the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell something at a fixed price before or on a set date. Because the owner can walk away, options have lopsided payoffs: limited loss for the buyer, potentially large gains. They can insure a portfolio, generate income, or make a leveraged bet, and they are priced by some of the most elegant models in finance.

items: A call gives the right to buy the underlying at the strike price $K$. You buy a call if you expect the price to rise.
A put gives the right to sell at $K$. You buy a put to profit from a fall or to insure shares you own.
The buyer (holder, long) pays a premium up front. The seller (writer, short) receives the premium and takes on the obligation.
American options can be exercised any time up to expiry (most US stock options); European options only at expiry (most index options, such as on the S&P 500).
A US listed stock option contract covers 100 shares, so a premium quoted at \$3.00 costs \$300.

blocks.text: At expiry, with the underlying at $S_T$:

Profit is payoff minus the premium paid. A call with strike 100 bought for \$4 breaks even at 104, loses at most \$4, and gains without limit above 104. A put with strike 100 bought for \$3 breaks even at 97 and gains at most \$97 (if the stock goes to zero). The seller's profits are the mirror image: a short call has limited gain and unlimited loss.

blocks.alt: Four small charts of profit at expiry against the stock price for a long call, a short call, a long put and a short put, each with the strike and break-even marked; the long call and long put have losses limited to the premium, the short call has unlimited loss.
blocks.caption: Profit at expiry for the four basic positions (strike K, premium paid or received).

blocks.text: Moneyness, intrinsic value and time value

items: In the money (ITM): exercising now would pay something: a call with $S > K$, a put with $S < K$.
At the money (ATM): $S \approx K$. Out of the money (OTM): a call with $S < K$, a put with $S > K$.
Intrinsic value: what exercising now would pay, $\max(S - K, 0)$ for a call.

Time value (extrinsic value) = premium − intrinsic value: what you pay for the chance that the option becomes more valuable before expiry. It is largest at the money, grows with time to expiry and with volatility, and decays to zero at expiry (time decay, faster in the final weeks).

blocks.text: Volatility is the key input. An option's value comes from the asymmetry: big moves in your favor pay a lot, big moves against you cost no more than the premium. So the more the underlying is expected to move, the more an option is worth, calls and puts alike. The market's estimate of future volatility, backed out of option prices, is the implied volatility; the VIX index measures it for the S&P 500 over the next 30 days.

A call plus cash equal to the present value of the strike has exactly the same payoff at expiry as a put plus the stock: both are worth $\max(S_T, K)$. Two portfolios with identical payoffs must cost the same (for European options on a stock without dividends):

This put-call parity pins calls and puts together. If it fails, traders buy the cheap side and sell the dear one. It also shows you can build any one of the four (call, put, stock, bond) from the other three: a long stock plus a long put is a 'synthetic' call plus a bond.

items: Insurance: a protective put limits the loss on stocks you own, like an insurance policy with a deductible (the gap to the strike) and a premium.
Income: selling covered calls on stocks you own collects premium in exchange for giving up gains above the strike.
Leverage: a call costs a fraction of the stock, so the percentage gain on a rise is much larger, and the percentage loss on a small fall can be total.
Defined-risk bets on direction or volatility: spreads, straddles and condors (see Option Strategies).

blocks.text: Most options bought by individuals expire worthless or are sold at a loss. Short-dated out-of-the-money calls are lottery tickets: cheap, exciting, and priced so that on average the buyer loses. Implied volatility has also tended to exceed later realized volatility (the variance risk premium), which favors option sellers on average but exposes them to rare large losses.

items: Employee stock options and restricted stock units (RSUs) are part of pay in many companies.
Warrants are long-dated calls issued by a company; exercising them creates new shares.
Embedded options: callable bonds (the issuer holds a call), convertible bonds (the holder holds a call on the stock), the prepayment right in a mortgage (a call the borrower holds).
Real options: the right to expand, delay or abandon a project, valued with the same ideas.

blocks.title: Break-even
blocks.text: You buy a call with strike 50 for \$2.50 and a put with strike 45 for \$1.20, on different days, on the same stock. Where does each break even at expiry, and what is the most each can lose?
solution: Call: breaks even at $50 + 2.50 = \$52.50$; the most it can lose is the \$2.50 premium (\$250 per contract).
Put: breaks even at $45 - 1.20 = \$43.80$; most it can lose is \$1.20 (\$120 per contract).

blocks.title: Intrinsic and time value
blocks.text: A stock is at \$108. A call with strike 100 and two months to expiry costs \$10.50. What are its intrinsic and time values? What will its time value be at expiry?
solution: Intrinsic $= 108 - 100 = \$8$; time value $= 10.50 - 8 = \$2.50$. At expiry time value is zero, so if the stock is still \$108 the call is worth \$8, and the buyer loses \$2.50.

blocks.title: Put-call parity
blocks.text: A non-dividend stock is at \$100. A one-year European call with strike 100 costs \$10.45 and the interest rate is 5% (continuous). What should the matching put cost?

blocks.title: Leverage
blocks.text: A stock is at \$50. You can buy 100 shares for \$5,000, or 10 call contracts (1,000 shares' worth) with strike 50 for \$2 each (\$2,000). At expiry the stock is at \$56, then in another case at \$51. Compare the returns.
solution: At \$51: shares gain \$100 (2%); calls pay \$1,000, a loss of \$1,000 (−50%) though the stock rose.
